notes.meaning: Jehoram son of Ahab began his twelve-year reign over the northern kingdom of Israel while Jehoshaphat was in his eighteenth year as king of Judah. His older brother Ahaziah had died without having a son, so Jehoram took the throne in the capital city of Samaria. He ruled during a stormy time when Israel was sliding deeper into trouble.

Jehoram did evil in God's eyes, yet he was not quite as bad as his wicked father Ahab and mother Jezebel. He took away the large stone pillar set up to worship the false god Baal. However, he only removed it from public display rather than destroying Baal worship completely, showing that his reform was only skin-deep.

Even though Jehoram removed the pillar of Baal, he held tightly to the worship of the golden calves started long before by King Jeroboam. Jeroboam had set up those idol shrines at Bethel and Dan to keep the northern tribes from traveling to Jerusalem to worship. Jehoram kept this false religion for political power, proving his heart was not truly devoted to the Lord.

King Mesha of Moab was a wealthy sheep rancher who was forced to pay heavy taxes to the king of Israel. Every year he had to send one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams. In the ancient world, subject nations often paid their tributes using the livestock and crops they produced.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: An ancient inscribed monument called the Moabite Stone, found in 1868, confirms King Mesha's rule and describes how Israel had dominated Moab and demanded heavy tribute during this era.

notes.meaning: As soon as King Ahab died, King Mesha rebelled by refusing to send any more sheep or wool to Israel. Ahaziah had been too sick and weak during his short reign to do anything about it. This left the problem for Jehoram to handle as soon as he took the throne.

King Jehoram moved quickly to prepare for war by counting and gathering all the fighting men in Israel. He wanted to march against Moab right away to force them back under his control. His first major test as king was to stop this rebellion before other nations followed Moab's example.

Jehoram sent messengers to King Jehoshaphat of Judah, asking him to join the war against Moab. Jehoshaphat agreed completely, promising his own soldiers and horses just as he had once done for Jehoram's father Ahab. Judah also wanted to punish the Moabites, who had invaded Judah's territory not long before.

When Jehoshaphat asked which way the army should attack, Jehoram chose the path leading through the desert of Edom. This southern route let them bypass Moab's heavily defended northern borders and pick up soldiers from Edom along the way. Yet it was a dangerous choice because it meant leading thousands of men and beasts through a dry wasteland.

The kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom set out together on a seven-day winding march through the wilderness. Edom was under Judah's control at the time, so its ruler went along as their ally. The journey took longer than planned, and soon there was no water left for the soldiers or their pack animals.

King Jehoram threw his hands up in despair and blamed the Lord for their trouble. He cried out that God had brought all three kings into the desert just to let Moab destroy them. A guilty conscience often makes people blame God for disasters caused by their own foolish plans.

Instead of giving up, Jehoshaphat asked if there was a true prophet of the Lord nearby so they could seek God's direction. An officer of Israel answered that Elisha was present with the army, describing him as the man who used to pour water on Elijah's hands to wash them. Jehoshaphat should have sought God before starting the war, but he rightly turned to Him in their hour of crisis.

Jehoshaphat recognized that Elisha was a true prophet who spoke the real word of the Lord. Instead of ordering the prophet to come to them, all three kings showed great respect by walking down to Elisha's tent themselves. Facing desperate need can quickly humble powerful leaders before God's servants.

Elisha gave a sharp rebuke to King Jehoram, asking why he was coming to him instead of consulting the false prophets of his father Ahab and mother Jezebel. Jehoram pleaded with Elisha not to turn them away, saying it was the Lord who had brought the three kings into this deadly trap. Elisha wanted the king to realize that false idols are completely useless when real trouble comes.

Elisha took an oath before the living Lord of Hosts that he would not even look at Jehoram if he were alone. He agreed to help only because he had deep respect for Jehoshaphat, who faithfully served the true God. Ungodly people often receive mercy and blessing simply because they are in the company of God's people.

Elisha called for a musician who could play the harp. The soothing, worshipful music calmed the prophet's spirit after his angry words to wicked Jehoram and prepared his heart for prayer. As the harpist played, the power and inspiration of the Lord's Spirit came upon Elisha.

Elisha delivered God's command to dig ditches and pits all over the dry valley. The thirsty soldiers had to do the hard work of digging before they saw a single drop of rain. God often asks His people to take steps of faith and prepare room for the blessing He plans to give.

The Lord promised that the army would feel no wind and see no rain, yet the dry valley would suddenly fill with fresh water. A storm would fall far away out of sight, sending a flood down the dry stream bed to fill the trenches. There would be plenty of water for all the soldiers, their horses, and their cattle.

Elisha assured the kings that filling the desert with water was a very small thing for Almighty God to do. Beyond saving them from dying of thirst, the Lord was also going to hand the entire army of Moab over to them. God often gives far greater answers to prayer than people even think to request.

The prophet foretold that the allied armies would crush Moab's cities, cut down their good trees, plug up their springs, and ruin their best fields with stones. This was a prediction of how totally Moab would be brought low for its rebellion and evil ways. God was about to break the pride and power of Moab completely.

The next morning, at the exact time when priests offered the morning sacrifice in Jerusalem, water suddenly poured in from the direction of Edom. The water flooded the dry ground and filled all the freshly dug trenches. God timed this miracle to honor the hour of true worship at the temple.

When the people of Moab heard that three kings were marching to attack them, they sounded the alarm across the nation. Every man old enough to strap on armor was called up and posted along the southern border. They took their stand ready to defend their country against the invaders.

The Moabite soldiers woke up early and looked across the valley just as the morning sun rose. The early red sunlight reflected off the water in the trenches, making it look as red as blood. Since the Moabites knew that the valley had been dry the day before, they never dreamed the pools could be water.

The Moabites jumped to the conclusion that the three allied armies must have turned on one another and fought to the death. Thinking the battlefield was full of corpses, they shouted to one another to rush in and grab the loot. Their greedy overconfidence blinded them to the danger ahead.

The Moabites rushed into the camp in total disorder, only to find the Israelite army alive, armed, and ready for battle. The Israelites attacked them fiercely and sent them running in terror. Israel chased the fleeing soldiers straight across the border and into the heart of Moab's homeland.

The allied armies marched through Moab, tearing down fortified towns, stopping up freshwater springs, and cutting down trees. Every soldier picked up stones and tossed them onto fertile farmland until the fields were ruined. Only the walled city of Kir-haraseth was left standing, and slingers surrounded it to strike the defenders on its walls.

When King Mesha realized he was trapped and losing the siege, he gathered seven hundred of his finest swordsmen for a desperate breakout. He tried to cut his way through the ranks of the king of Edom, thinking that was the weakest spot in the enemy line. However, the Edomite forces held firm, and the Moabite king was pushed back into the city.

In horrific desperation, King Mesha took his oldest son, who was next in line for the throne, and offered him as a burnt sacrifice on top of the city wall in full view of everyone. A terrible sense of indignation and dread fell upon the besiegers, leading the allied armies to break camp and return to their own lands. The awful deed showed the darkness of pagan worship when driven to absolute despair.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate whether the great fury that fell upon Israel was God's judgment against the allies for pushing the siege to such an atrocious end, or the intense anger and fighting spirit of the horrified Moabite survivors.
